title: Screwworm Wildlife Monitoring: The Blind Spot on Feral Hog Lines
content:
TL;DR: Screwworm wildlife monitoring should cover the feral hog lines that cattle checks miss. Keep livestock inspection and agency reporting separate from trap operations, then use live trap-site observation to track movement, maintain sounder logs, and decide when a field visit or closure command is needed.

Cattle monitoring and wildlife monitoring are not the same job. During a New World screwworm alert, landowners may inspect herds, check fresh wounds, and follow a reporting path. Meanwhile, feral hogs can keep moving through back fences, brush lines, wallows, and baited trap sites with no one watching.

USDA APHIS explains that screwworm targets live animals with fresh wounds, not feces. Trap-site observation can show where feral hogs and other wildlife are moving. It cannot confirm screwworm. If you suspect screwworm in cattle, wildlife, or feral hogs, contact USDA APHIS and your state agricultural extension office.

Why Cattle and Wildlife Coverage Diverge

Managed livestock are on a schedule. A team can walk a pasture, examine an animal, document a wound, and involve the right professional. That routine gives cattle checks a structure. Feral hogs do not. They travel at night, cut through cover, fight, cross fences, and return to bait when the property is quiet. A daylight check does not tell you what used the creek crossing, fence gap, or trap line overnight.

That gap is where screwworm wildlife monitoring becomes practical. It does not mean inspecting every animal. It means building observation around places where wildlife already concentrates, then keeping those records separate from livestock inspection and agency reporting.

The Hog Line Is a Practical Observation Point

They sit where rooting, trails, wallows, bait, water, and cover pull sounders back to the ground. A trap-site feed can show when hogs arrive, how many are using the site, whether other wildlife is working the bait, and whether pressure changes after a catch.

Live trap-site monitoring gives a current view without sending someone to every corridor after dark. It also keeps the purpose clear: the system supports remote trap monitoring, sounder capture timing, and field decisions. It does not replace agency reporting or animal health expertise.

What Observation Can and Cannot Show

  • Confirm when feral hogs are using a monitored trap site
  • Help separate hog activity from other wildlife around bait
  • Show whether the full sounder is committed before closure
  • Support a dated trap log with location, movement, and catch notes
  • Give your team context for a conversation with USDA APHIS or extension contacts

A camera cannot show larvae enough to confirm an infestation. It cannot tell you to treat an animal. Keep suspected cases on the reporting path. Use the trap log for what it can support: date, time, place, species, estimated sounder size, catch outcome, and movement changes.

Align Cattle Protocols With Trap-Line Coverage

Run the two tracks side by side. Keep livestock checks, wound concerns, and reporting contacts in their own process. Add a daily remote review for active trap sites, especially when an alert has the team paying closer attention to animal movement.

Assign one person to review the feeds and a backup who can send the closure command. Keep a weekly sounder log. Note when bait disappears, when hogs hold outside the trap, when the complete sounder settles inside, and when a field visit is needed.

A wild hog trap camera system should frame the entrance, the trap interior, and the approach area. The HogEye steel camera is built for that trap-site job, giving the team a live view for closure decisions. Setup references are available in camera resources.

Trapping Outcomes Matter to Both Tracks

Whole-sounder removal reduces the number of wide-ranging hogs crossing the property. Remote monitoring helps the team wait until the full sounder is inside and settled before sending the closure command. Early closure can catch the bold hogs and educate the survivors. Those survivors may avoid the trap, shift to another corridor, or use a route with no camera. Partial capture can make both trapping and wildlife observation harder.

After a catch, review the feed and the log. Did the full sounder enter? Did another group replace it? Did activity move toward a fence gap, water edge, or secondary bait site? Those answers keep the wildlife side of the property from depending on guesswork.

When to Escalate

Escalate when you see something that raises concern. Record what you saw, where you saw it, and when. Then contact USDA APHIS and your state extension office. Do not diagnose from footage. Do not treat from footage.
